A content delivery network is a way of storing copies of a website's content in many different places around the world, so people can get that content quickly no matter where they are. Without one, every request for a page, image, or video has to travel all the way back to the origin server, which is the original computer where the website's files live permanently. That trip can be slow if the origin server is far away. To fix this, copies of the content get placed on servers scattered across many cities, known as edge locations, positioned close to where people actually are. When someone requests something and a nearby edge location already has a saved copy ready to hand over, that is called a cache hit, and it means the content arrives almost instantly instead of making the long journey back to the original source. Think of it like a chain of bakeries that all sell bread baked at one central factory, but each neighborhood shop keeps fresh loaves on hand so nobody has to travel across town for a simple loaf. When a shop is out of stock, it fetches more from the factory, refills its shelf, and future customers get the fast version. This system makes browsing feel snappier, reduces strain on the original source, and keeps things working smoothly even when many people request the same content at once.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|------|---------------|-----------------|
| Origin server | The original computer storing a website's real files | It is the ultimate source everything else copies from |
| Edge location | A nearby server holding copies of content | It shortens the distance content has to travel |
| Cache hit | A request answered instantly from a nearby copy | It makes browsing feel fast and reduces delays |
| Content delivery network | The whole system of connected copy-holding servers | It keeps popular sites fast and reliable worldwide |
